newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Brussels airport operator urges better access.
newsitem.headline: Brussels airport operator urges better access.

text.p: Brussels international airport operator BATC said on Tuesday net profit jumped 160 percent to 644 million francs ($18.3 million) in 1996 but urged authorities to improve access to the airport to sustain further growth.
Turnover rose to 5.2 billion francs ($148 million) from 4.6 billion ($131 million) a year earlier, BATC said in a statement.

"In the name of our 14 million passengers a year we urge authorities to settle the taxi problem during rush hours...a better flow of traffic to and from the airport, parking lots, train links...and other challenges which stand in the way of a further growth of the airport," BATC CEO Pierre Klees said.
Brussels airport, for many years the butt of jokes about the hazards of air travel, inaugurated a new $674 million terminal building in December 1994.
The first terminal was built in 1958 with an annual capacity of six million passengers. The new terminal has boosted capacity to 21 millon passengers a year.

Klees, noting BATC was aware of the shortcomings of its infrastructure and improvements that could still be applied, added a further expansion of the airport could help create thousands of new jobs on top of the 20,000 directly linked to the airport activity.

General manager Mark Duyck said income rose due to an eight percent rise in passengers and a considerable rise of income from concessions and advertising now that the new passenger terminal had become fully operational.
He said costs had been cut as a number of posts linked to the move from the old to the new terminal had been scrapped.
Financial charges were cut by 130 million francs to 880 million ($25 million) due to paybacks of investment credits and a lower interest rates on financial markets.

BATC's board decided to pay 110 million francs ($3.1 million) in dividends to its shareholders -- the Belgian state via the Airways Direction with 47.5 percent and several institutional investors -- against 80 million in 1995.
